title: Flagged for Review
subtitle: Irregularities, unverified values, discrepancies and assumptions — published, not hidden
rule: A value that could not be confirmed from an official primary source is left BLANK on this site. It is never inferred, estimated or filled in from a secondary source. Every item below is reported with what was checked and what could not be confirmed. Items marked “needs review” do not block publication.

c: Individual-level vs household-level income for the $580 test

42 CFR §435.552(f)(2) and WIC §14005.69(e)(6) as amended by AB 2161 both measure the income test on the MAGI-based household budget. But ACWDL 25-30 instructs counties that “All individuals must independently meet the participation criteria; one individual’s compliance cannot be used to satisfy another’s requirement”, and defines the income criterion as “an individual’s total gross income for a month”. CMS’s own IFC deck adds that an agency “must use a reasonable method to allocate work hours between members of the household”. The interaction between a household MAGI test and an individual compliance determination is not spelled out. Left unresolved — neither reading is assumed.
Does managing your own rental property count as “work”?

CMS defines work as work in exchange for money, in-kind work, and unpaid work other than community service, and states in the IFC preamble that self-employment — “starting a business, owning a business, or as an independent contractor” — meets that definition and that the hours count. No official CMS, DHCS or county document uses the terms “landlord”, “rental property” or “property manager”. Applying the rule to self-managed rental real estate is an inference, not a documented rule. Value left blank — confirm with the county before relying on this pathway.
Does full-time Kalshi event-contract trading count as “work” or self-employment?

No official guidance was located — not from CMS, not from DHCS, not from any county, not from the IRS. Two obstacles: (a) it is unresolved whether CFTC event contracts are “securities” within IRC §475(c)(2), so the IRS trader framework may not apply at all; (b) even where it applies, IRS Topic No. 429 says trader gains “aren’t subject to self-employment tax”. Left blank.

Kalshi is a CFTC-regulated event-contract exchange; its own documentation describes a Profit and Loss statement plus 1099-INT / 1099-MISC / 1099-B / 1099-DA. Nothing in Kalshi’s official documentation calls its products futures. This matters because IRC §1256 treatment (Form 6781, the 60/40 split, year-end mark-to-market) depends on the contract being a regulated futures contract or another listed §1256(b) instrument. The tax characterisation of Kalshi event contracts is unresolved by the IRS — no Revenue Ruling, Notice or regulation was located. Four competing treatments appear only in unofficial practitioner literature (Section 1256; capital asset; ordinary income on Schedule 1 line 8z; gambling income). None is published here as verified.
Seasonal-worker 6-month averaging is likely unavailable — and state guidance is broader than the federal cross-reference

42 CFR §435.552(a)(7) and WIC §14005.69(e)(7) allow a 6-month average only for a “seasonal worker, as described in section 45R(d)(5)(B)” of the IRC. The official U.S. Code text defines that as a worker who “performs labor or services on a seasonal basis as defined by the Secretary of Labor, including workers covered by section 500.20(s)(1) of title 29, Code of Federal Regulations and retail workers employed exclusively during holiday seasons.” A full-time trader or full-time property manager does not fit. However, ACWDL 25-30 describes the same criterion more loosely as being for “individuals with fluctuating income over a six-month period”, and the DHCS member letter says “people whose hours change frequently or who have seasonal jobs”. The state guidance is broader than the federal statutory cross-reference. Left unresolved.
“California permanent resident” — citizenship / immigration status assumed

This analysis assumes a U.S. citizen residing in California. If the person is a lawful permanent resident or holds another status, H.R.1 §71109 (federally funded full-scope Medicaid narrowed from October 1, 2026), Covered California’s January 1, 2027 restriction of Marketplace financial help to certain immigrant groups, DHCS’s January 1, 2027 fee-for-service transition and July 1, 2027 premium requirement may all apply. No conclusion is drawn for any status other than U.S. citizen.
Other California safety-net programs (CMSP, Medi-Cal Access Program, CDPH condition-specific programs)

These programs exist, but their current eligibility rules, income limits and application channels were not verified against an official primary source in this session. All such values are left blank rather than filled in from secondary sources.

The official IRS Revenue Procedure setting 2027 applicable percentages was not retrieved in this session. Third-party summaries circulate figures. Those figures are not published anywhere on this site; the value cell is left blank pending retrieval of the IRS document.

FTB’s personal health-care-mandate page (last updated 09/15/2026) still publishes “Sample penalty amounts for 2025” — $950 per adult, $475 per child, or 2.5% of gross income above the filing threshold. 2026 amounts are not published there. A Covered California document titled “2026 Individual Shared Responsibility Penalty Calculation” (dated 2025-08-25) references “$420 per month for an individual” for calendar year 2026; that figure could not be reconciled with FTB’s flat-amount method within this session, so it is not published as a 2026 penalty amount. Value left blank.
DHCS copayment threshold “$15,560 a year” does not match any published HHS poverty guideline

DHCS’s official consumer page says the October 1, 2028 copayment applies to adults 19–64 who “Make more than $15,560 a year”. Federal law (H.R.1 §71120) attaches cost-sharing to expansion adults with income above 100% FPL. Published 100% FPL for one person: 2025 = $15,650; 2026 = $15,960. $15,560 matches neither. It may be a transposition typo, a figure based on an unpublished future-year guideline, or a household-size-specific number. Reported exactly as quoted, with the discrepancy noted; no corrected value is substituted.
January 1, 2027 vs March 2027 — when the rules actually bite in California

Four official statements coexist: (1) the federal statute and CMS require implementation no later than January 1, 2027; (2) ACWDL 25-30 says counties will not assess members with an application date of December 31, 2026 or prior until their next scheduled renewal in 2027, and that the provision applies to all applications submitted on or after January 1, 2027; (3) the DHCS consumer page says six-month eligibility checks start March 1, 2027; (4) the DHCS member outreach letter in MEDIL I 26-25 tells members the rules “will not go into effect until March 2027” while separately saying the 6-month renewal rule begins January 2027. All four are reported as quoted. The safe planning assumption is that the obligation can attach to any application filed on or after January 1, 2027.
Federal Register HTML URL path format (slashes vs hyphens)

An earlier retrieval attempt returned “404 Not Found” when date segments in the Federal Register URL were hyphenated (/documents/2026-06-03/...). Re-verified on 2026-10-19 (session arena/b02db1f0): the canonical slash-separated URL (/documents/2026/06/03/2026-11094/...) returns HTTP 200 with the full 135-page rule, alongside the official govinfo PDF and the eCFR codified text.

The Federal Register document record states: “This document was corrected by a document published on 06/29/2026” (FR Doc. C1-2026-11094, 91 FR 39028, pages 39028–39031). Live-fetched and read line by line on 2026-10-19 (session arena/b02db1f0): the June 29, 2026 correction solely republishes corrected regulatory text for 42 CFR § 435.557 (verifying compliance) and 42 CFR § 435.558 (noncompliance procedures) beginning at 91 FR 33476 (already integrated into the eCFR as of 10/15/2026) and does not alter §§ 435.551–435.556, the 80-hour standard, or the $580/month MAGI-based income pathway.
ACWDL 25-30 is expressly preliminary and predates the federal rule

The letter carries the notice: “This ACWDL represents preliminary guidance and is subject to change based on developing federal policy guidance and state legislative changes.” It was issued December 30, 2025 — before CMS published the interim final rule on June 3, 2026, and before AB 2161 was chaptered on September 14, 2026. Where ACWDL 25-30 differs from the IFC, the regulation or WIC §14005.69 as amended controls. No superseding ACWDL had been located as of 2026-10-18.
DHCS impact estimates vary widely between official documents

The DHCS H.R.1 Implementation Plan (Jan/Feb 2026) estimates “up to 233K Medi-Cal members will lose coverage by June 2027, 1 million by Jan 2028, and 1.4 million by June 2028”. A CalHHS Connect webinar deck (October 2025) estimates “up to 3 million Medi-Cal members may lose coverage”. The DHCS FY 2026-27 Budget Act Highlights projects “43,000 in 2026-27 and 1.1 million” thereafter. All three are reported as quoted with their dates; none is presented as the estimate.

Multiple third-party tax sources state that P.L. 119-21 §70433 raised the general 1099-MISC / 1099-NEC information-reporting threshold from $600 to $2,000 for payments made in 2026, indexed from 2027. The IRS instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC (Rev. December 2026) do reference $2,000 in an example, but the statutory section number and effective date were not verified against the statute or an IRS primary document in this session. Not published as a verified figure; left blank.
Medi-Cal asset limits do NOT apply to the MAGI adult group — but sources conflate them

DHCS’s consumer page describes asset limits of $130,000 through 6/30/2027 then $21,000 / $31,000 from 7/1/2027, and lists “More than one house or vehicle” among counted assets. Those limits apply to the groups DHCS describes on that page — age 65+, people with disabilities, nursing-home residents, and families over income under federal tax rules (Non-MAGI). For MAGI-determined eligibility, 42 CFR §435.603(g)(1) is explicit: the agency “must not apply any assets or resources test”. This site states both, with the scope of each clearly labelled, so a property owner in the MAGI adult group is not misled into thinking rental real estate disqualifies them.

AB 2208 (Stefani) would set a $0.01 Medi-Cal copayment for the expansion population and restore 3 months of retroactive coverage. Official legislative history: 08/13/26 — “In committee: Held under submission.” Type of measure: “Active Bill – In Committee Process.” It is reported here as pending, never as enacted. Advocacy summaries describing it as California’s response must not be read as current law.
Two different versions of WIC §14005.69(e)(6) are in circulation

The version added by SB 164 (Stats. 2026, Ch. 27, §75) lists illustrative income types (“earned income, unemployment benefits, state disability insurance, retirement income, or dividends”). The version as amended by AB 2161 (Ch. 209, Stats. 2026) replaces that list with “using modified adjusted gross income (MAGI)-based financial methods … for their individual MAGI-based household budget”. Both are quoted with their source. Neither limits the test to earned income. The leginfo code page retrieved 2026-10-18 still displays the SB 164 wording; the AB 2161 chaptered text is linked separately.

The DHCS member letter and MEDIL I 26-25 both direct members to dhcs.ca.gov/workrules. Retrieval on 2026-10-18 shows that URL redirects to the “Medi-Cal Changes” page rather than serving a dedicated work-rules page. This site links the resolved destination and records the redirect so a manual reviewer is not surprised.
No official guidance on in-kind, rent-free property management

42 CFR §435.552(b) counts “work in exchange for goods or services (‘in-kind’ work)”. A person who manages a property in exchange for free or reduced rent would appear to fall inside that definition, but no official CMS or DHCS example addresses it. Left blank.
The Kalshi PnL statement is explicitly not a tax document

Kalshi states the PnL statement and its contents “are not tax advice … each member should consult with a tax professional … and is responsible for ensuring the accuracy of all returns”, and that “if no 1099 forms appear in your account, it is likely because you did not meet the IRS thresholds required for issuance”. None of the four 1099s Kalshi lists reports event-contract trading profit. A person relying on the $580 income pathway should therefore be able to document MAGI from their own records plus any 1099s actually received, because the county may request documentation when its reliable data sources are unavailable or “not reasonably compatible” (42 CFR §435.557(b)(2)).
This site contains no legal, tax or medical advice

Every page carries a plain-language disclaimer and links only to primary sources. Nothing here substitutes for advice from a licensed California attorney, a CPA or enrolled agent, DHCS, a county eligibility worker, or a Covered California certified enroller.

sections.title: Repository review findings
sections.intro: The repository was reviewed line by line. The entire pre-existing content was one 12-byte line.

c: The repository contained no code, no data, no documentation and no configuration other than a 12-byte README.md. There was nothing to audit for factual accuracy in the pre-existing content.
git ls-files returned exactly COORDINATION.md and README.md at review time; commit history was a single commit, 4f79596 “Initial commit” (buffedlizard55-lab, 2026-10-11).
README.md is 12 bytes and has no trailing newline. Cosmetic only.
The repository name MaltaProj9 has no discoverable relationship to its subject matter; nothing in the repository explains it.
cat README.md — the heading is the only occurrence of the name.
There was no .gitignore, so generated artefacts risk being committed.
ls -a at review time showed only .git, README.md. A .gitignore was added in this session.
GitHub Pages was not enabled and no publishing workflow existed.
There was no COORDINATION.md, although the working instructions require one as the shared task board.
Created and pushed as the first commit of this session, a643881.

Conclusion. No irregularities of substance were found in the pre-existing repository content, because there was essentially none. Every factual claim on this site was therefore newly authored and newly verified against an official primary source rather than inherited and audited.
